transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-12-04
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Sophie (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Aisha (Redwood Platform), Daniel (Orion CTO), Priya (Orion SRE), Ethan (Orion ML), Maya (Orion Infra)

Summary: Technical deep dive focused on p95/p99 tail latency for streaming and non-streaming paths, KV cache warm/cold behavior, batching trade-offs, quantization impacts on latency vs quality, and network hop overheads for Private/VPC and on-prem deployments. Customer wanted concrete suggestions and to align on benchmark plan for a POC.

Topics: p99 vs p95, streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache warm/cold, prefix caching, batching windows, quantization profiles (int8/4bit), network hops (cross-AZ, NAT), TLS and TCP handshake costs, cold start variability, model fallbacks and canary routing.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sophie: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll run through p99 tail latency stuff and then leave time for action items, quick intros?
[00:18] Daniel: hi Daniel here, CTO at Orion, we've been seeing p99 spikes for our chat assistant in peak hours — sometimes 1.2s baseline but spikes to 3.4s on longer prompts which is killing UX.
[00:30] Marcus: thanks Daniel, can you give a quick run-down of your stack and where Redwood sits in it?
[00:38] Priya: sure, requests come from our frontend to a routing layer, then to an API gateway, we call Redwood Hosted today for inference. We use 1024 token max, typical prompt 400 tokens, about 30 rps average but bursts to 300 rps.
[00:55] Ethan: also we tried a quantized variant (4-bit) in test infra, saw token throughput improve but tail got worse occasionally which was surprising.
[01:08] Marcus: ok good context — three big axes: model execution latency, batching/pipeline latency, and network/hop-induced latency. We'll step through each and look for p99 sources.

[01:22] Marcus: first, streaming vs non-streaming — are you using streaming on the client?
[01:28] Priya: yes websocket streaming for chat, but we also have some server-side non-streamed calls for summarization.
[01:34] Marcus: streaming reduces perceived latency for users because tokens arrive early, but tail behavior can actually be dominated by a single token generation stall. On the server, if a request is waiting for a batching window, that wait time shows up at p95/p99. We tie batching window and batching size to latency SLOs.
[01:52] Marcus: for example, a 20ms batching window is great for throughput but can add 20ms per request; if jitter causes a late arrival, that late arrival impacts the entire batch. Do you have server metrics about batching wait times?
[02:06] Priya: we don't see batching metrics in our current logs, just token/sec and average lat.
[02:12] Marcus: that's a gap — action: we'll surface batching wait histograms in the POC.

[02:22] Marcus: second big area: KV cache warm vs cold. Are you using prefix caching or long-lived sessions?
[02:29] Ethan: we use session-based KV cache with typical chat sessions of 8-12 turns. But when a user comes back after 10 minutes, cache misses spike.
[02:36] Marcus: cold KV cache means the model must re-run the prefix which is linear in prefix length — that shows up as tail spikes. On Redwood, we aim to keep sessions sticky on the same instance to keep KV hot; but when autoscaling or failover evicts a session, you see a cold miss.
[02:54] Aisha: we also saw that a cold miss combined with a big batch can cause p99 to skyrocket because that single request does extra work. Our runtime's KV checkpointing reduces cold-miss penalty by streaming restored KV and overlapping compute, but it's workload-dependent.
[03:11] Daniel: can you quantify warm vs cold cost?
[03:15] Marcus: ballpark: warm next-token step ~8-12ms for this model on V100-equivalent; cold prefix replay for 400 tokens maybe 400-800ms depending on compute, so p99 often dominated by cold replays or rehydration.
[03:28] Ethan: that matches our observations — the 3.4s spikes usually correlate with new sessions or after an autoscale event.

[03:35] Marcus: third — quantization. You saw mixed results with 4-bit?
[03:40] Ethan: int4 improved throughput but p99 sometimes worse; memory was lower but occasionally the compute kernel had tail latency variance.
[03:46] Marcus: yes, lower precision helps throughput and average latency, but kernel selection and instruction set behavior can increase variance. Some kernels are slower on small batch sizes or for certain sequence lengths. For small-batch, int8 path might actually be faster and more predictable than int4 depending on runtime and hardware.
[04:04] Marcus: recommendation: run side-by-side p95/p99 for int8 vs int4 and include sequence-length buckets (<=128, 129-512, 513-1024). We'll do that in the benchmark.

[04:18] Maya: network hops — we are in AWS VPC with NAT and cross-AZ load balancer, could NAT or cross-AZ routing add jitter?
[04:25] Marcus: absolutely. TLS handshakes, cross-AZ hops, NAT gateway cold translations can add 10-50ms per request intermittently. For streaming, TCP keepalives matter — if connections are being torn down and re-established you pay TLS/TCP costs.
[04:40] Aisha: for Private deployments we recommend keeping clients and inference nodes in the same AZ, use internal load balancers, and enable long-lived connections. If on-prem, you want an internal gRPC/WebSocket ingress so you don't repeatedly cross network boundaries.

[04:54] Daniel: we are considering Private (VPC) vs Dedicated; will Private reduce p99?
[04:59] Marcus: Private reduces external network hops and gives you direct control over NICs and placement, which generally lowers median and tail. Dedicated hosted can be very good too but depends on your routing layer and whether you can keep sessions sticky.

[05:12] Marcus: some quick debugging heuristics: 1) correlate p99 spikes with instance events/autoscale/failover 2) check KV cache hit rate over time 3) inspect batching wait time histograms, 4) look at kernel-selection logs (int4 vs int8) 5) correlate with cross-AZ CPU/IO wait.

[05:30] Priya: on instrumentation, what do you recommend we capture right now?
[05:33] Marcus: at minimum: per-request timestamps for gateway receive, gateway forward, batch queue enter/exit, first token emit, last token emit, KV cache hit/miss flag, kernel path, instance id. That will let us attribute latency to network vs runtime vs cache.
[05:52] Ethan: ok we'll add those traces. For POC benchmarking, what's the harness?
[05:57] Marcus: Redwood has a benchmark harness that can replay production-like traffic with preserved inter-arrival patterns and sequence lengths. We'll run p95/p99 for three configs: hosted int8, hosted int4, and Private (same HW) with long-lived connections and sticky sessions.

[06:14] Sophie: also want to set expectations: improving p99 often requires combination: reduce network variance (network changes), tune batching windows, ensure KV session stickiness, and pick a quantization that has stable kernels for your seq length distribution. There is rarely a single knob.
[06:31] Daniel: about client streaming — we've seen users complain even when median is fine; any quick wins there?
[06:36] Marcus: yes — send partial tokens as soon as available, use client-side heuristics to render partials. On the server, prioritize low-latency requests by using separate low-latency routing pool for small-reply requests. Redwood supports route-based policies so you can split short answers vs long generation.

[06:55] Priya: what's the impact of batching size at high QPS? We saw average latency increase with larger batch sizes but tail seemed stable?
[07:01] Marcus: at high QPS, batches fill quickly so batching wait time is small, which reduces impact. Tail issues at high QPS more often come from contention on instance resources or network I/O. At low QPS, batching window dominates. We can suggest dynamic batching windows — shrink window when traffic drops.

[07:20] Aisha: on the runtime side we can enable kernel-level prefetch and overlap KV restore with compute to shave cold-miss penalty. We'll propose a config that trades a small memory footprint for faster rehydration.

[07:32] Ethan: curious about metrics we should compare in the benchmark beyond p95/p99?
[07:36] Marcus: include tail histograms, every-quantile plots, per-token latency distribution, batching wait distribution, KV hit ratio over time, and percent of requests hitting cold-replay path.

[07:48] Daniel: are there any platform-level limits that could cause big p99 spikes we might have missed?
[07:52] Marcus: yes — GC pauses on host, noisy neighbors on multi-tenant hardware, and OS-level interrupts. For Dedicated/Private, single-tenant reduces noisy neighbor risk. We also saw issues where platform autoscaler created ephemeral instances that didn't have warmed kernels — initial requests pay JIT or kernel compile costs.

[08:10] Sophie: let's recap next steps, action items — Marcus will run bench and gather kernel-path p95/p99 for int8/int4 buckets; Marcus/Aisha will produce batching histograms; Priya will share traffic samples; Sophie will send security docs and schedule POC.
[08:26] Daniel: sounds good, also can Redwood share a suggested config for session stickiness and NAT settings?
[08:31] Marcus: yes we'll include recommended LB sticky settings, keepalive values, and a suggested network diagram for Private.

[08:40] Priya: one last question — how do you validate quality regression when you change quantization?
[08:45] Marcus: we tie quality monitoring to evals and prompt sets; we'll run a sample of your live prompts through each quantized model and calculate delta metrics (perplexity proxies, and a small manual eval set for hallucination/regression). That runs alongside latency bench so you can make informed tradeoffs.
[09:05] Daniel: ok great.

[09:08] Sophie: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the bench results and SOC2 pack.
[09:12] Meeting ends.

Notes/References: Marcus referred to internal kernel-selection logs and a benchmark harness link (sent after meeting). Customer asked for SOC2/ISO docs and a network diagram for Private. We noted that session stickiness, KV hotness, and batching windows are highest-leverage for p99.
